title: Engineering ethics and the NSPE code
note: The NSPE Code's first Fundamental Canon tells engineers to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public. The others require working only within competence, truthful public statements, faithful service to employers and clients, avoiding deceptive acts, and honorable, lawful conduct.

read.title: Holding the public paramount
text: Engineers make decisions that strangers trust with their lives: the people crossing a bridge, flying in an airliner, or sleeping in a high-rise never meet the engineer, but they depend on that person's judgment. That is why engineering is a licensed profession with a code of ethics.

The National Society of Professional Engineers sets out six Fundamental Canons. The first says engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public. The rest require them to work only within their competence, to speak publicly only in an objective and truthful way, to act as faithful agents of their employers and clients, to avoid deception, and to conduct themselves honorably and lawfully.

Faithfulness to an employer has limits. When an engineer's judgment is overruled in a way that endangers life or property, the Code says to notify the employer or client and any other appropriate authority. Conflicts of interest must be disclosed, and an engineer may seal only plans prepared under that engineer's own direction and control.

These rules were not written in the abstract. The Hyatt Regency collapse cost its engineers their licenses, and the Challenger launch decision shows what can happen when engineers' warnings are set aside.

q.q: What does the first NSPE canon place above all else?
What should an engineer do if overruled in a way that endangers life?
o: Notify the employer or client and other appropriate authority

q.q: Which plans may an engineer seal?
o: Plans prepared under the engineer's own direction and control
